title: THE STOPPED CLOCK (STUB)
question: HOW DID A STOPPED CLOCK GIVE THE KILLER AN ALIBI?
briefing: Placeholder case for testing the desk. Harold Brandt, clock dealer, found dead in his back office at 0705 hours.
The wall clock came down with him. It stopped at 9:15. Everybody likes a clock like that.
Close it by morning. — Capt. R. Iles

files.title: Incident report
lines: 0705 hours. Responded to Brandt Clocks, 14 Harrow Lane. The assistant, Mira Holt, found Harold Brandt dead in the back office.
A wall clock lay face down beside him, glass broken, hands stopped at [[9:15|t0915]].
Back door bolted inside. Front door locked; the only other key is with the nephew, {{Leo Brandt|leo}}.
back: Canvass, flat 14A: a neighbour, {{Mrs. Odile Fenn|fenn_tape}}, heard a crash in the evening. Statement taped at 0750.

files.title: Item 3: the wall clock
files.cover: Item No. 3 · recovered from the floor
lines: Hands at 9:15. Glass broken outward. Pendulum unhooked.
back: Lab pencil: eight-day movement, [[fully wound|wound]]. It did not run down.

files.title: Leo Brandt
lines: Says he left the shop at nine and walked home alone. Nobody saw him after 9:00 PM.
back: Holds the second key to the front door.

files.title: Mira Holt
lines: Locked up at 8:00 PM, she says, and went straight to the 8:30 show at the [[Rialto Cinema|cinema]].
back: Kept her ticket stub. Showed it before anyone asked.

files.title: Interview: Odile Fenn
files.speaker: ODILE FENN
lines: DET.: Tell me about the noise.
I had the wireless on. The eight o'clock news had just finished, so it was [[ten past eight|t0810]].
Then a crash from Mr. Brandt's, like glass going. I thought he'd dropped a clock. He was always dropping something.
After that? Nothing. Not a sound all night.

files.title: Pathologist's note

unlock.text: The pathologist, on the line: 'Between six-thirty and eight-thirty last night. Not nine-fifteen. I've allowed for the radiator.'

lines: Cause of death: (a) blunt force injury to the head. Manner: pending.
Estimated time of death: between [[6:30 and 8:30 PM|window]], allowing for the radiator the first officer switched off.

monologue.text: A clock stopped at nine-fifteen. Sometimes a case hands you the time on a plate.
Leo. Owes his uncle money, holds a key, and walked home alone. They always walk home alone.
A crash at ten past eight. Probably a clock off a shelf. That shop is full of them.
Leo, at nine-fifteen. It fits. I should feel better about it than I do.
No. Something in that sentence is wrong, and it might be me.
Six-thirty to eight-thirty. Then what was that clock doing at nine-fifteen?

parts.heading: FIRST THEORY
parts.text: {a} killed Harold Brandt at {b}, when the clock came down.
parts.wrong_but_expected: The clock's time and the one man with no alibi for it: the theory the scene was built to give.

parts.heading: THE CLOCK
parts.text: The clock fell at {a}. {b} set its hands to 9:15, knocked it down, and left for the {c}.

overturn.text: The pathologist's window shuts before nine. The clock never stopped at the time of death: somebody chose what it would say.

truth.headline: THE CLOCK DIDN'T STOP. IT WAS STOPPED.
truth.how_it_seemed_impossible: The clock pinned the death to 9:15, when Leo had no alibi and Mira was in a cinema with a stub to prove it.
how_it_was_possible: Mira struck Harold a little before eight.
She turned the clock's hands to 9:15 and knocked it from the wall. A fallen clock shows whatever its hands say.
At ten past eight the neighbour heard the crash: the clock coming down an hour before the time it showed.
Then Mira walked to the 8:30 show and kept the stub where it would be seen.

rerun.text: Fully wound: it never ran down. Its hands were set by hand, to a time someone picked.
The crash at ten past eight was the clock itself.
A stub shown before anyone asked is an alibi that was prepared.
